newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: British mercenary leaders says no regrets over PNG.
newsitem.headline: British mercenary leaders says no regrets over PNG.

text.p: Tim Spicer, British army colonel-turned-mercenary, sat ignominously in a tiny Papua New Guinea court on Monday, but the former Scots Guard was adamant he had no regrets about his failed mercenary mission.
"I don't think we would have done anything different. It's unfortunate the way things have turned out," Spicer said.
Only a week ago he was the dashing commander of a group of hardened mercenaries paid by the government to crush an uprising and recapture a giant copper mine on the island of Bougainville.
Now, behind a rickety timber railing that served as a dock, 44-year-old Spicer looked more tired than dashing.
It was a long way from his luxury office in London's fashionable King's Road, but Spicer had been in sticky situations before and had always managed to find a way out.
He'd dealt with the Serbs in Bosnia, the Iraqis in the Gulf War and helped push the Argentines out of the Falkand Islands.

And the two books he took with him into the dock could still be useful: "Victory At Any Cost", about the Vietnam War, and a biography of Ian Fleming, creator of Britain's most famous action man, James Bond, 007.

Dressed in blue jeans, blue shirt and sailing shoes without socks, the former British officer, honoured with the Order of the British Empire for his tours in Northern Ireland, waited for charges to be read out on two minor firearm offences.
He stood up and pleaded a confident "not guilty" to both charges, one of possessing an unlicensed Russian Makarov 9mm pistol, and one of possessing 41 rounds of ammunition.

The mission of the 70 mercenaries, mostly veterans of guerrilla wars in Southern Africa, was to end the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville, an island 800 km (500 miles) north-east of Port Moresby, and recapture the Panguna mine.
On Monday he sat alone in Boroko District Court Two after falling foul of the local soldiers he was supposed to have led into battle.
Outside beyond a high razor-wire fence stood crowds of locals and a pack of foreign journalists jostling for a glimpse of the mercenary who has left this nation in political turmoil.
Spicer's fellow "dogs of war" were thrown out of the country last week by rebellious army officers who are also demanding Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan resign over the mercenary deal.

Those same officers want Spicer to remain so that he can testify at an inquiry into the US$36 million contract between the government and his British-based military consultancy Sandline International.

Magistrate Boio Kidu refused to release Spicer's passport to allow him to leave the country, setting an April 8 trial date. He said Spicer will have to spend another two weeks in Port Moresby as a guest of British High Commissioner Bob Lowe.

"Due to the seriousness of this case and what has happened in our country the passport is to be withheld," Kidu, flanked by 40 cartons of "South Pacific Bitter" beer, told a courtroom crowded with police and journalists.
As Spicer jostled with reporters to get to a Land Rover provided by the British High Commission, he said: "There is nothing wrong with the activities of Sandline."

Later at a more controlled press conference inside the high commission, Spicer said he had no regrets about his mercenary mission to Papua New Guinea, adding he would be happy to testify at an inquiry starting April 1.
"It was all done in good faith as far as I am concerned and it's unfortunate the way it has turned out," Spicer said.
"I don't want to get involved in a debate about the rights and wrongs of the issue. I have no bad feelings about the Papua New Guinea government or the people of Papua New Guinea."
Spicer, who said he had received US$18 million, half his contract fee, for the failed mission, again stressed Sandline was a legitimate business.
"I don't have a problem with what I do, I don't have a problem with what my company does," he said.
